Alleviate

/uh-LEE-vee-ate/ — rhymes with 'abbreviate' · verb

Hear It

What It Means

To alleviate something, like pain or a problem, is to make it less severe or easier to bear.

An ice pack helped alleviate the swelling in her ankle.

Worked Example

The teacher allowed students to submit their essays two days late, which greatly alleviated the stress that had been building throughout the week.

Alleviate is precise because the teacher didn't remove the assignment or solve the problem entirely—the essay still had to be written. What she did was make it less severe and more manageable. That's exactly what alleviate means: reduce the pain or difficulty, not eliminate it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

mitigate: To mitigate is to make harmful effects less severe — engineers mitigate flood damage, courts mitigate penalties. It aims at the harm a thing causes. To alleviate aims at the person carrying the burden: pain, stress, or worry made easier to bear. Mitigate softens consequences; alleviate lightens suffering.

diminish: To diminish something is to make it smaller or weaker — the medicine diminished the fever, the criticism diminished her confidence. It reports shrinkage and nothing more. To alleviate is to lighten a burden so it is easier to bear; the sufferer feels relief, not just reduction.

relieve: To relieve pain or pressure is to take it off someone so they feel free of it, at least for a while — the way medicine relieves a headache. To alleviate is more modest: the problem stays, but its weight is reduced to something bearable. Relief removes; alleviation lightens.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

aggravate: to make pain or problems worse

exacerbate: to intensify something that is already bad

Where it sits · how much of the pain is removed — ease → improve → alleviate → eliminate

ease vs. alleviate: Ease is the gentlest word on this scale: to ease pain is to lessen it slightly, while to alleviate it is to lighten the burden in a real, noticeable way.

improve vs. alleviate: Improve is weaker than alleviate: improving a bad situation makes it somewhat better overall, but alleviating it means clearly reducing the suffering it causes.

eliminate vs. alleviate: Eliminate is stronger than alleviate: to alleviate a problem is to make it easier to bear, but to eliminate it is to remove it completely.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — al-

Prefix — al-: to, toward (an assimilated form of Latin ad-)

Root — levi

Root — levi: light in weight (from Latin levis, 'light')

Suffix — -ate

Suffix — -ate: to make (verb-forming) (Latin)

Put it together

Put it together: Al- ('to,' an assimilated form of Latin ad-) + levi ('light in weight,' from Latin levis) + -ate ('to make') literally means 'to make light' — to alleviate pain or a problem is to lighten its weight so it becomes easier to carry.

Use the root in a new word: elevate

Use the root in a new word: elevate: A crane can elevate a heavy beam — lift it as if it were light — using the same Latin root lev- ('light in weight') found in alleviate, 'to lighten a burden.'
